---
title: "Counts, percentages and rates"
description: "How to choose and interpret common forms of BNR statistics."
---

Counts, percentages and rates use numbers differently. Choosing the right one depends on the question being asked.

## Why this matters

The same underlying events can produce several correct statistics, each with a different interpretation.

| Statistic | Main question | Typical denominator |
|---|---|---|
| **Count** | How many events or people were recorded? | None |
| **Percentage** | What share of an eligible group had a characteristic or outcome? | Eligible events or people |
| **Population rate** | How frequently did events occur relative to a population? | Resident population |
| **Ratio** | How does one quantity compare with another? | A comparison quantity |

## Counts

A count is a total. It is often the clearest measure of service burden, but comparisons can be misleading when population sizes differ.

For example, 100 events in a population of 100,000 represent a different frequency from 100 events in a population of 300,000.

## Percentages

A percentage expresses a part of a defined whole:

$$
\text{Percentage} = \frac{\text{number in the selected group}}{\text{eligible total}} \times 100
$$

Always check the denominator. A case-fatality percentage among hospital events is not a percentage of the whole population.

## Population rates

A rate relates events to the population and a period:

$$
\text{Rate per }k = \frac{\text{events}}{\text{population}} \times k
$$

BNR commonly uses \(k=100,000\) for CVD event rates. The multiplier makes small frequencies easier to read; it does not change the underlying comparison.

## Crude and age-adjusted rates

A crude rate uses observed totals. An age-adjusted rate combines age-specific rates using a standard age distribution. This helps compare populations or periods with different age structures.

Age-adjusted rates are comparison tools. They are not the actual number of events and should not be multiplied by the local population to estimate a count.

::: {.callout-tip title="A simple comparison rule"}
Compare statistics only when the event definition, source coverage, period, denominator and adjustment method are compatible.
:::

## What to remember

- Counts describe volume.
- Percentages describe a share of an eligible group.
- Population rates improve comparisons across differently sized populations.
- Age adjustment addresses age structure, not every source of bias or uncertainty.
